indicator.subject: Mathematics
indicator.sub_strand: Data Collection, Organization, Presentation, Interpretation and Analysis
indicator.content_standard: Create, label, and interpret line graphs to draw conclusions.
indicator.objective: Determine whether a given set of data can be represented by a line graph (continuous data) or a series of points (discrete data) and explain why

skills.description: Decide whether data is continuous or discrete.
Explain why data is continuous or discrete.
Choose between a line graph and a scatter of points.

misconceptions: Thinking all tables should be line graphs

questions.stem: Is the number of pupils in a class discrete or continuous data?
hints: Pupils are counted in whole numbers.
You cannot have half a pupil.
questions.explanation: The number of pupils is discrete because it takes whole-number values.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is continuous because it changes over time.

questions.stem: Is the height of a growing plant continuous or discrete data?
hints: Height can take any value, e.g., 5.2 cm, 5.25 cm.
questions.explanation: Height is continuous because it can take any value within a range.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is discrete because we write whole numbers sometimes.

questions.stem: A table shows the number of matchsticks used to make 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 squares. Is this discrete or continuous?
hints: Matchsticks are counted in whole numbers.
questions.explanation: The number of matchsticks is discrete.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is continuous because the pattern continues.

questions.stem: A table shows temperature recorded every minute. Is this discrete or continuous?
hints: Temperature can be between values, e.g., 25.5°C.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is discrete because it is recorded at intervals.

questions.stem: A table shows the number of people in the immediate family of P6 students (1, 2, 3, 4...). Is this discrete or continuous?
hints: People are counted in whole numbers.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is continuous because it varies.

questions.stem: A pupil records distance travelled by a bicycle every 5 minutes. Is this discrete or continuous?
hints: Distance can be between values, e.g., 3.5 km.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is discrete because it is recorded at intervals.

questions.stem: A table shows the number of goals scored by a football team in each match. Is this discrete or continuous?
hints: Goals are counted in whole numbers.
questions.explanation: The number of goals is discrete.
questions.misconception: Thinking it is continuous because it changes.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The temperature at 3.5 minutes can be read from a line graph.' Is this possible?
hints: Temperature is continuous, so intermediate values exist.
questions.explanation: Both time and temperature are continuous, so intermediate values can be estimated.
questions.misconception: Thinking time is discrete because we write whole minutes.

questions.stem: Explain why the number of oranges in a basket is discrete data.

criteria.description: States that oranges are counted in whole numbers
Explains that you cannot have part of an orange

questions.explanation: Oranges are counted in whole numbers; you cannot have a fraction of an orange, so the data is discrete.

questions.stem: Explain why the mass of a bag of rice is continuous data.

criteria.description: States that mass is measured, not counted
Explains that mass can take any value within a range

hints: Can rice have a mass of 5.25 kg?
questions.explanation: Mass is measured and can take any value, so it is continuous.
questions.misconception: Thinking mass is discrete because we round it.

questions.stem: Explain why the number of matchsticks in a pattern is discrete data.

criteria.description: States that matchsticks are counted in whole numbers
Explains that you cannot have part of a matchstick

questions.explanation: Matchsticks are counted in whole numbers, so the data is discrete.
questions.misconception: Thinking the pattern makes it continuous.

questions.stem: A pupil says: 'The temperature at 2.5 minutes is 35°C.' Explain why this is possible on a line graph.

criteria.description: States that temperature and time are continuous
Explains that intermediate values can be estimated from the line

hints: Can temperature be between two readings?
questions.explanation: Both time and temperature are continuous, so the line between plotted points represents intermediate values.
questions.misconception: Thinking the line only connects whole-number points.

questions.stem: Why is a line graph suitable for showing temperature over time but not for showing the number of pupils in different classes?

criteria.description: Number of pupils in different classes is discrete/categorical

questions.explanation: Temperature over time is continuous, so a line graph is appropriate. Class sizes are discrete categories, so a bar chart is better.
questions.misconception: Thinking any data can use a line graph.

questions.stem: A table shows water temperature recorded every 2 minutes. Can a line graph be used? Explain.

criteria.description: Explains that a line graph can show the trend and estimate between readings

hints: Temperature can be measured between the 2-minute intervals.
questions.explanation: Yes, because temperature is continuous, a line graph can show the trend and allow estimation between readings.
questions.misconception: Thinking recording at intervals makes it discrete.

questions.stem: Which graph is best for showing how temperature changes over 10 minutes?
hints: We want to show change over time.
A line graph connects points to show a trend.
questions.explanation: A line graph is best for showing change over time.
questions.misconception: Choosing a bar chart, which is better for comparing categories.

questions.stem: Which graph is best for showing the number of pupils who like different fruits?
questions.explanation: A bar chart is best for comparing categories.
questions.misconception: Choosing a line graph, which implies continuity.

questions.stem: A pupil wants to show the number of matchsticks used for patterns 1 to 5. Should they use a line graph or a scatter of points?
hints: Matchsticks are counted in whole numbers.
questions.explanation: Since matchsticks are discrete, a series of points is more appropriate than a continuous line.
questions.misconception: Joining the points with a line as if the data were continuous.

questions.stem: A pupil records the mass of a baby every month for a year. Which representation is best?
hints: We want to show growth over time.
questions.explanation: A line graph is best because mass is continuous and we want to show growth over time.
questions.misconception: Using a pie chart for continuous data.

questions.stem: A table shows the number of goals scored in 5 matches. A pupil draws a line graph joining the points. What is wrong?
options: Goals are discrete, so points should not be joined
The line graph is always correct
The graph needs a pie chart
hints: Goals are counted in whole numbers.
There is no meaning to 2.5 goals between matches.
questions.explanation: Goals are discrete; joining the points implies continuous data, which is misleading.
questions.misconception: Thinking a line always makes the graph better.
